title: Enabling the Emergence of Leadership
author: Nick Hart
summary: The second post in Hart's three-part series moves from critique to mechanism, asking what leaders actually do if leadership is a social process rather than a role. He organises the answer around three interacting concepts: the conditions, the interactions and the interpretations. For conditions he draws on Complexity Leadership Theory's three functions, administrative leadership as the operational backbone of routines and predictability, adaptive leadership as the capacity to respond to new challenges, and enabling leadership as the management of the tension between them. Interactions carry the weight of the argument, since administrative clarity only lands if what is communicated is discussed and negotiated, and adaptive responses only appear if people feel safe enough to challenge assumptions and have time to experiment. Hart then lists the systems through which leaders can raise the quality of interaction, from how meetings run and how CPD is organised to quality assurance methodology and how teachers plan. The third concept, interpretation, holds that sense making determines what people do next, and that what staff think is happening matters more than what leaders intended to communicate. A change in assessment policy, he notes, is read through staffroom conversation, workload history and prior trust. Interpretation closes the loop, feeding back into the conditions for the next round of interactions.
points: The three functions of Complexity Leadership Theory give leaders a language for a real tension: structures that keep a school coherent versus the adaptive responses that improve it.
Hart's practical claim is that leaders enable interactions indirectly, by designing the systems that make good interactions more likely, rather than by exhorting people to collaborate.
The assertion that what people think is happening matters more than what leaders intended to communicate reframes communication failures as interpretation problems rather than message problems.

Sense making is characterised as inherently social and emotionally loaded, shaped by memory, trust and context as much as by information, which is why a new initiative is judged on what came before it.
Leaders cannot control interpretation but can influence it through sense giving, which Hart says works in both command-and-control and relational registers.
quotes: They assume that schools are complicated and ultimately controllable systems, where the right people making the right decisions will yield the right results. Leadership, in those models, is usually something done by individuals to others, defined by role, enacted through instruction and measured by delivery.

Administrative leadership is the operational backbone of routines, expectations, clarity and predictability. Adaptive leadership is the capacity to respond to new challenges. And enabling leadership is managing the tension between the two; creating the conditions in which adaptive responses can emerge without letting go of the structures that keep the school coherent.
Leadership doesn’t reside in individuals, it emerges in the interactions between them.

Adaptive leadership only brings solutions to new challenges if people feel safe enough to raise difficult questions, challenge assumptions and have the intellectual and temporal capacity to experiment with new approaches.
The meaning that we collectively make of the conditions we’re working in through our interactions are shaped not just by information but by emotion, memory, trust and context.

In schools, the administrative leadership of formal communication (briefings, policies, plans) sits on top of a deeper layer of lived interpretation. What people think is happening often matters more than what leaders intend to communicate.
A change in assessment policy isn’t just a change in process, it’s interpreted through staffroom conversations, workload history and prior trust.
